clinicalPearls: Oxidising drugs and chemicals convert haemoglobin iron to the ferric state, forming methaemoglobin that cannot carry oxygen
The hallmark is cyanosis that does not improve with supplemental oxygen, often with chocolate-brown blood
There is a characteristic saturation gap, with pulse oximetry reading falsely and the arterial blood gas oxygen tension appearing normal
Common precipitants include topical local anaesthetics such as benzocaine, dapsone, nitrites and aniline dyes
Methylthioninium chloride (methylene blue) is the specific antidote for significant or symptomatic cases
Methylene blue may be ineffective or harmful in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, where alternatives are needed
reference.pathophysiology: Methaemoglobin forms when the iron in haemoglobin is oxidised from the ferrous to the ferric state, which cannot bind oxygen and also shifts the oxygen dissociation curve so remaining normal haemoglobin releases oxygen less readily. Oxidant drugs and chemicals overwhelm the physiological reducing systems, chiefly cytochrome-b5 reductase, that normally keep methaemoglobin low. The result is functional anaemia and tissue hypoxia despite adequate arterial oxygen tension, producing cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen.
additionalDifferentials: Hypoxaemia from cardiac or pulmonary disease
Congenital methaemoglobinaemia (enzyme or haemoglobin M variants)
additionalInvestigations: Co-oximetry to measure the methaemoglobin fraction directly
Arterial blood gas demonstrating the saturation gap
Careful drug and chemical exposure history
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase status before or alongside methylene blue
Haemolysis screen where oxidant injury is significant
redFlags: Signs of tissue hypoxia such as chest pain, altered mental state or acidosis
Ongoing exposure to the causative agent
reference.prognosis: Mild cases resolve once the offending agent is stopped, and symptomatic cases usually respond rapidly to methylene blue; severe or unrecognised cases can cause serious hypoxic injury.
pitfalls: Being reassured by a normal arterial oxygen tension despite cyanosis
Giving methylene blue in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
Failing to identify and remove the causative oxidant
Confusing it with primary cardiopulmonary hypoxaemia
management: Immediate removal or cessation of the offending oxidant agent such as benzocaine, dapsone, nitrites or aniline dyes
Methylthioninium chloride (methylene blue) as the specific antidote for significant or symptomatic methaemoglobinaemia
Supportive high-flow oxygen while the methaemoglobin fraction is being reduced
Check glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase status, avoiding methylene blue in deficiency and using ascorbic acid, exchange transfusion or hyperbaric oxygen instead
Monitor response with serial co-oximetry rather than pulse oximetry
Escalate to exchange transfusion for severe or refractory cases
